about.summary: While the price is above its 200-day average, buy when the MACD line crosses above its signal line (momentum turning up); sell when it crosses back below, or at a 10% loss.
about.why: Gerald Appel created MACD in the late 1970s; the crossover of the MACD and signal lines is its classic buy and sell signal, and it is taught in standard texts such as Murphy's. Adding the 200-day filter, a common practitioner refinement, takes only signals in the direction of the long-term trend.
about.caveats: MACD is built from moving averages, so it lags and gives many whipsaw signals in sideways markets. Crossovers on their own have weak evidence; treat this as a timing tool inside a trend.
references: Appel, G. (2005). Technical Analysis: Power Tools for Active Investors. FT Prentice Hall.
Murphy, J. J. (1999). Technical Analysis of the Financial Markets. New York Institute of Finance.
